reader_question: How did fiscal 2026’s receipts and outlays add up to the deficit?
grade_line: Documented: the Treasury’s monthly statement of federal receipts and outlays
title: Federal outlays of $7,395.8 billion in fiscal 2026 ran past receipts of $5,403.3 billion, leaving a deficit of $1,992.5 billion.
reading_guide: Read from the top. Each receipt adds to the running total, the bar for all receipts starts again from zero, and each outlay takes its amount away; the last bar is the shortfall, the deficit.
measure_line: Federal receipts by source and net outlays by budget function, billions of dollars, nominal, fiscal year 2026 (October 1, 2025 to September 30, 2026), United States
notes: Two outlay lines are negative in the Treasury’s statement, so they add to the running total: commerce and housing credit, $15.5 billion, and undistributed offsetting receipts, $155.0 billion, money agencies collect that counts against spending.
Social Security, Medicare, net interest, health and national defense each took more than $900 billion.
Fiscal 2026 figures come from the September 2026 statement and may change in the Treasury’s year-end report.
alt: A waterfall from fiscal 2026’s nine receipt sources, which add to $5,403.3 billion, through 19 outlay functions to a deficit of $1,992.5 billion. Individual income taxes, $2,845.5 billion, and payroll taxes, $1,754.3 billion, bring in most receipts; Social Security, $1,667.1 billion, is the largest outlay.
